replying_to: Replying to Transport Clustering: Solving Low-Rank Optimal Transport via Clustering
display_title: Official Review of Submission21593 by Reviewer njmU

summary.value:
Low-rank optimal transport (OT) aims to approximate the optimal transport plan by constraining it to have small nonnegative rank, effectively routing mass through a few latent anchors. This structure naturally induces a clustering of the supports—points that share an anchor form co-clusters across the source and target distributions. While the motivation for low-rank OT is scalability, the optimization problem itself is nonconvex and NP-hard, in contrast to the convex linear formulation of classical OT. However, practical algorithms for low-rank OT often lead to scalable approximations in practice.

This paper takes the inverse view: instead of discovering clusters through a low-rank constraint, it first computes a full OT map to register the supports, then clusters the induced correspondences to identify anchors, and finally reconstructs a low-rank coupling consistent with this clustering. The resulting “transport clustering’’ approach reduces low-rank OT to a single generalized k-means problem and achieves a provable constant-factor approximation (between 2× and 3×, depending on the cost function) to the best rank-K OT cost for metric or kernel costs.

The presentation is somewhat confusing. The introduction motivates low-rank OT as a scalable alternative to full OT, yet the proposed method begins by computing a full OT map, which appears contradictory. The paper does not clearly emphasize that the full OT is computed only once to extract reusable structure for downstream efficiency. As written, it reads as if the “scalable’’ approach is computationally harder, whereas the real contribution is to show that—despite the NP-hardness of low-rank OT—one can obtain a constant-approximation solution through a simple clustering reduction built from a single OT computation.

strengths.value: The paper tackles an interesting compression problem where the goal is to incur a one-time OT computation cost in order to learn clusters that enable faster and more structured future OT computations. The connection to generalized k-means is elegant, and the constant-approximation result is novel and theoretically clean.

weaknesses.value:
The presentation is lacking in clarity; it takes significant effort to piece together the motivation and the sequence of reductions. The introduction could better separate what is meant by “scalability” in this context.

The experiments do not include the initial full rank OT computation cost.

questions.value: How does this paper relate to the result of Indyk and Price (STOC 2011), where k-median clustering provides a sparse, relative approximation of the Earth Mover’s Distance? Could their compression-based approach be viewed as an implicit low-rank or clustered approximation to OT?

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission21593 by Reviewer njmU

comment.value:
We thank reviewer `njmU` for their positive evaluation of the manuscript and address their questions/comments point-by-point:

> The presentation is lacking in clarity; it takes significant effort to piece together the motivation and the sequence of reductions. The introduction could better separate what is meant by “scalability” in this context.

We agree with your assessment regarding the clarity of presentation and have also addressed this comment in the meta response.  The discussion on scalability is confusing and introduced in the context of prior work [1, 2, 3] which emphasizes low-rank OT as a "scalable alternative" to full-rank OT. We agree this contextualization is slightly disingenuous as low-rank OT is NP-hard while full-rank OT can be solved in polynomial time. We have updated the manuscript to shift the emphasis and plan to further edit the  manuscript for clarity in the camera ready version.

> The experiments do not include the initial full rank OT computation cost.

This is an important point. In the camera ready version, we will update our experiments to include the full-rank OT cost as a point of comparison. We note all runtimes reported in the current work are inclusive of the  full-rank OT solve time.

> How does this paper relate to the result of Indyk and Price (STOC 2011), where k-median clustering provides a sparse, relative approximation of the Earth Mover’s Distance? Could their compression-based approach be viewed as an implicit low-rank or clustered approximation to OT?

Thank you for sharing this paper. If we understand correctly, this work [5]    finds a sparse _marginal_ $\\mu^{\\star}$ within a constant-factor of the optimal $K$-sparse $\\mu\_{K}$ (i.e. a distribution on $K$ atoms), i.e.: $W(\\mu^{*}, \\mu)\\leq C\\min\_{\\mu\_{K}} W(\\mu\_{K}, \\mu)$. In contrast, we are _given_ two marginals and optimize for a coupling subject to a rank constraint.  Further, the referenced work concerns (i) an $\\ell_{1}$ cost on a grid $\\{1,\ldots, n\\}^{2}$ in $\\mathbb{R}^{2}$ and (ii) is only provided a linear sketch of the distribution marginals.  Interestingly, the low-rank sub-couplings $\\mathbf{Q}, \\mathbf{R}$ implicitly yield a pair of $K$-sparse barycenters on $X$ and $Y$, i.e. the $K$ points with weight $\mathbf{g} \in \\Delta_{K}$ supported on the points $\\mathbf{Q}^{\top} \\text{diag}(1/\\mathbf{a}) \\mathbf{X} \in \\mathbb{R}^{K \times d}$ and $\\mathbf{R}^{\\top} \\text{diag}(1/\\mathbf{b}) \\mathbf{Y} \in \\mathbb{R}^{K \times d}$, though these are not marginals. For the camera ready revision,  we intend to further investigate the relationship  between transport clustering and the techniques  used in [5].

replying_to: Replying to Transport Clustering: Solving Low-Rank Optimal Transport via Clustering
display_title: Official Review of Submission21593 by Reviewer oGJd

summary.value:
The paper builds upon the ideas introduced in [1], which establish a connection between the optimal transport problem and the k-means clustering algorithm through a non-negative factorization of the transport plan. A key distinction, however, is that while [1] focuses on clustering a single dataset, the present work extends these concepts to the co-clustering of two datasets — a framework the authors refer to as Transport Clustering. Since solving the low-rank optimal transport problem is NP-hard, the authors propose a multi-step approximation method and derive theoretical approximation ratios under various metric settings, including negative, kernel, and general metrics.

[1] Scetbon, Meyer, and Marco Cuturi. “Low-rank Optimal Transport: Approximation, Statistics, and Debiasing.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (2022): 6802–6814.

strengths.value: The paper is very well written and addresses an important problem which could be used in the development of computational tools for domain registration and alignment. The proposed methods provide a strong foundation for bridging distributional differences between datasets through transport-based formulations. Furthermore, the techniques presented in the paper could be extended to design large-scale, class-conditioned domain registration frameworks, enabling more structured and semantically meaningful alignment across complex datasets.

weaknesses.value: One major source of confusion for me is the incessant switching between assignment form partition formulations of low rank optimal transport problem. In the main body results are stated in assignment form, whereas proofs in appendix are written in partition formulation, which makes it harder for reader to follow the proofs.

questions.value: While authors of the paper applied their technique to synthetic data, co-clustering on CIFAR-10 and cellular Transcription, I wonder if it could be applied to small domain alignment problem.

We completely agree. The conflict is that the assignment form presented in the main text is consistent with existing literature [1, 2, 3] on low-rank OT, while the analysis is significantly simpler written in partition form. In the camera ready version, we will revise the main text to avoid this switching.

> While authors of the paper applied their technique to synthetic data, co-clustering on CIFAR-10 and cellular Transcription, I wonder if it could be applied to small domain alignment problem.

Thank you for the suggestion to evaluate transport clustering on a small domain-alignment task. We created a 1,000-by-1,000 CIFAR-10 benchmark using the same images under mild appearance shifts (color/contrast jitter) and applied `TC`, `LOT`, and `FRLC` with rank $K = 10$, the same as the number of class labels. As shown in Table 4, TC achieves the best AMI/ARI among the three methods and the lowest transport cost, demonstrating that our approach extends naturally to domain-alignment settings.

replying_to: Replying to Transport Clustering: Solving Low-Rank Optimal Transport via Clustering
display_title: Official Review of Submission21593 by Reviewer 8esR

summary.value: Optimal Transport (OT) has been a popular technique in machine learning in recent years. Its low-rank variant has also received wide attention due to computational and statistical advantages. This paper proposed a method for low-rank OT called \emph{transport clustering} that approximately solves the low-rank OT problem with a clustering subroutine. Approximation error is theoretically analyzed. Experiments demonstrate the advantages over existing low-rank OT methods.

strengths.value:
1. The transport clustering method is elegantly designed.

2. The authors provide theoretical proofs for the approximation factors.

3. Experimental results such as Figure 2 illustrate its advantages over existing low-rank OT methods.

weaknesses.value:
1.  When the marginal distributions are arbitrary distributions, the authors outline an extension for the method (Line 267-Line 276), but the paper seems to lack theoretical guarantees for such an extension. For example, does problem (9) even have a solution when the marginal distributions are arbitrary? How robust is this extension?

2. The method relies on existing full-rank OT solvers like the Hungarian algorithm or the Sinkhorn algorithm to register the cost matrix, which undermines the computational efficiency of low-rank OT. The Hungarian algorithm may take prohibitive runtime for large-scale real-world problems, and it may not be easy to extract a permutation matrix from the transport plan obtained by the Sinkhorn algorithm. In addition, in some applications, it may be unnecessary to consider low-rank OT after computing full-rank OT.

3. The considered tasks in Sec. 5 seem a bit too traditional.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission21593 by Reviewer 8esR

comment.value:
We thank `8esR` for their response and address their questions point-by-point:

> When the marginal distributions are arbitrary distributions, the authors outline an extension for the method (Line 267-Line 276), but the paper seems to lack theoretical guarantees for such an extension. For example, does problem (9) even have a solution when the marginal distributions are arbitrary? How robust is this extension?

Yes, the problem indeed admits a solution for arbitrary marginals, as discussed in [1, 2]. Recalling Problem (9), we have
$$\\min\_{\\substack{\\mathbf{Q}, \\mathbf{R} \\in \\Pi\_{\\bullet}(\\mathbf{u}\_n,\\,\\mathbf{g}) \\\\
    \\mathbf{g} \\in \\Delta\_K
    }}  \\,\\, \\langle\\mathbf{C}, \\mathbf{Q}\\,\\mathrm{diag}(1/\\mathbf{g})\\,\\mathbf{R}^{\\top} \\rangle\_F.
$$
The extension for arbitrary marginals $\\mathbf{a}$ and $\\mathbf{b}$ is
$$\\min\_{\\substack{\\mathbf{Q} \\in \\Pi(\\mathbf{a},\\,\\mathbf{g}), \\\\ \\mathbf{R} \\in \\Pi(\\mathbf{b},\\,\\mathbf{g}), \\\\
    \\mathbf{g} \\in \\Delta\_K
    }}  \\,\\, \\langle\\mathbf{C}, \\mathbf{Q}\\,\\mathrm{diag}(1/\\mathbf{g})\\,\\mathbf{R}^{\\top} \\rangle\_F.
$$
The above problem has a feasible solution for any $\\mathbf{g} \\in \\Delta\_K$ given by the outer-products $\\mathbf{Q}=\\mathbf{a} \\mathbf{g}^{\\top}$ and $\\mathbf{R}=\\mathbf{b} \\mathbf{g}^{\\top}$ satisfying $\\mathbf{Q 1}\_r = \\mathbf{a}, \\mathbf{Q}^{\\top}\\mathbf{1}\_n = \\mathbf{g}$ (resp. $\\mathbf{R}$). From [1, 2], the feasible set is compact and necessarily contains a minimum, so the problem is at least well-posed. While this is a well-defined problem, our analysis providing approximation guarantees for transport clustering are specialized to the Monge case rather than the Kantorovich case with arbitrary marginals. We believe a theoretical
analysis of the latter case would be a valuable direction for future work and have 
preliminarily added empirical results on this extension in Table 1, Meta Response. These results are described in detail in our second response to reviewer `UauS`.  In summary, our experiment suggests that the arbitrary marginal case with $n \\neq m$ exhibits 
similar empirical performance and robustness
to the Monge case presented in the manuscript.

> The method relies on existing full-rank OT solvers like the Hungarian algorithm or the Sinkhorn algorithm to register the cost matrix, which undermines the computational efficiency of low-rank OT. The Hungarian algorithm may take prohibitive runtime for large-scale real-world problems, and it may not be easy to extract a permutation matrix from the transport plan obtained by the Sinkhorn algorithm. In addition, in some applications, it may be unnecessary to consider low-rank OT after computing full-rank OT.

As noted in the meta response, the core contribution of transport clustering is not in scalability and we do not view transport clustering as offering complexity savings relative to prior work [1, 2, 3] on low-rank OT. For example, in Table 2 and Figure 7 (main text) we observed that the runtime of `TC` is notably higher than any existing low-rank OT solver due to the full-rank OT solve. However, we do not believe the increased computational complexity of our approach is problematic: low-rank OT is an NP-hard, non-convex optimization problem and existing approaches such as `FRLC` [3] or `LOT` [1] do not provide any guarantees on the quality of their solution. To clarify this point, in the revised manuscript we have  removed text that motivates low-rank OT as a scalable alternative to full-rank OT.

> The considered tasks in Sec. 5 seem a bit too traditional. 

Low-rank OT as an approach for co-clustering has made headway into areas such as vision and single-cell transcriptomics, but perhaps not enough for applications to more advanced tasks such as flow-matching. We agree that this is an exciting future direction that would demonstrate the value of low-rank OT for modern applications.

display_title: Official Review of Submission21593 by Reviewer UauS

summary.value: The paper proposes “transport clustering’’ (TC), which reduces the low-rank OT problem to a generalized $K$-means task by first registering the cost matrix with the optimal full-rank transport plan and then solving a single clustering subproblem. The authors obtain polynomial-time constant-factor guarantees—$(1+\gamma)$ for negative-type metrics and $(1+\gamma+\sqrt{2\gamma})$ for kernel costs—and instantiate the idea with mirror-descent (GKMS) and SDP-based solvers. In the experiments, TC outperforms prior low-rank OT methods on synthetic and real datasets.

strengths.value: The reduction from low-rank OT to a single clustering problem via cost registration is novel in my opinion, conceptually unifying co-clustering with $K$-means while providing constant-factor guarantees, leveraging mature toolboxes such as Lloyd iterations and SDP relaxations, and consistently improving transport costs over LOT, FRLC, and LatentOT in experiments—all of which makes for a genuinely novel and useful perspective on low-rank OT.

weaknesses.value: TC still requires a full OT solve up front, so the practical savings are unclear without runtime data; the constant-factor guarantees depend on assumptions and a small gap $\gamma$ that are not quantified empirically; registration for non-square or weighted marginals is only sketched (no experiments); implementation details, for example, ensuring positive column sums, initialization fairness, iteration counts are lack; the cost registration may create prohibitive memory demands.

questions.value:
- How sensitive is TC to errors in the transport registration? 
- Do the constant-factor guarantees still hold when $n\neq m$ or when the marginals are non-uniform? If so, can you illustrate Kantorovich registration with at least one experiment in that setting?
- Could you provide ablations where baseline solvers are initialized with the same transport-registration (e.g., feeding TC's clusters into LOT/FRLC) to isolate whether the gains come from the reduction or from better initialization?
- Since Algorithm~1 begins by solving a full OT problem, can you quantify the end-to-end complexity savings? In settings where the standard OT solve already dominates runtime, does the K-means reduction still offer any benefit?

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission21593 by Reviewer UauS

comment.value:
We thank `UauS` for their response and address their questions point-by-point:
> How sensitive is TC to errors in the transport registration?

Transport clustering is sensitive to the quality of the transport registration. We have added an experiment that assesses the sensitivity of transport clustering to the quality of
    the transport registration. In particular, we vary the entropy regularization parameter $\epsilon_i=10^{i}$ with magnitudes $i \in \\{-5, \cdots, 0, 1\\}$ for the Sinkhorn step of the transport clustering algorithm. Here, as $\epsilon_i$ increases (i.e. as the coupling moves away from optimal), the quality of the transport registration decreases and
    we obtain a higher final cost (see Table 2). Meanwhile, as $\epsilon_i$
    decreases the total final cost decreases, with a 5-order of magnitude gap in $\epsilon_i$ improving solution cost by a factor of two and a 7-order of magnitude gap improving the cost by a factor of three.

> Do the constant-factor guarantees still hold when or when the marginals are non-uniform? If so, can you illustrate Kantorovich registration with at least one experiment in that setting?

The proposed extension of Monge registration, Kanotorovich registration, does
    not currently come with theoretical guarantees. This is due to the simplicity of analyzing Monge registration as compared to Kantorovich registration, though we expect similar proof
    techniques to apply to the Kantorovich case. However, in the rebuttal we have provided preliminary empirical results for Kantorovich 
    registration (see Meta Response, Table 1) by fixing $n=1024$, varying $m \in \\{1024, 512, 256, 128, 64 \\}$, and applying transport
    clustering (`TC`) with Kantorovich registration to the 2-Moons and 8-Gaussians [4] dataset. The relative difference between `TC` and `FRLC` and `LOT` 
    is similar for both Monge and Kantorovich registration, even for $m$ over an order of magnitude different from $n$. For the camera ready revision, we intend to include an extended empirical analysis of
    Kantorovich registration.

> Could you provide ablations where baseline solvers are initialized with the same transport-registration (e.g., feeding TC's clusters into LOT/FRLC) to isolate whether the gains come from the reduction or from better initialization?

As noted in _Guarantees from Transport registered initialization with $K$-means and $K$-medians,_ by applying $K$-means to obtain the clusterings $\\mathbf{Q}\_X$ and $\\mathbf{R}\_Y$ and taking the minimum of the transport registered co-clusterings $(\\mathbf{Q}\_{X}, \mathbf{P}\_{\\sigma^{\\star}}^{\\top} \\mathbf{Q}\_{X})$ and $(\\mathbf{P}\_{\\sigma^{\\star}} \\mathbf{R}\_{Y}, \\mathbf{R}\_{Y})$
 already ensures a constant factor guarantee. If we denote this "best of two" initialization as $(\\mathbf{Q}\_{0}, \\mathbf{R}\_{0})$, any solver which reduces the low-rank OT cost from the initialization will maintain the constant-factor approximation. Thus, applying a low-rank OT solver such as `FRLC` or `LOT` with $(\\mathbf{Q}\_{0}, \\mathbf{R}\_{0})$ will also maintain the guarantee. We have added an ablation study in Table 3 to quantify the effect of using the transport registered initialization in another low-rank OT solver (`FRLC`). Transport registration of the initialization accounts for the majority of the practical improvement across the methods, which is as expected from the theory.

> Since Algorithm~1 begins by solving a full OT problem, can you quantify the end-to-end complexity savings? In settings where the standard OT solve already dominates runtime, does the K-means reduction still offer any benefit?

As noted in the meta response, the core contribution of transport clustering is not in scalability and we do not view transport clustering as offering complexity savings relative to prior work on low-rank OT. For example, in Table 2 and Figure 7 (main text) we observed that the runtime of `TC` is notably higher than any existing low-rank OT solver due to the full-rank OT solve. However, we do not believe the increased computational complexity of our approach is problematic: low-rank OT is an NP-hard, non-convex optimization problem and existing approaches such as `FRLC` [3] or `LOT` [1] do not  provide any guarantees on the quality of their  solution.

replying_to: Replying to Transport Clustering: Solving Low-Rank Optimal Transport via Clustering

comment.value:
**Meta Response.** The authors thank the reviewers for their positive evaluation of the manuscript and detailed feedback. In this meta-response, we
respond to two pieces of feedback shared by the four reviewers: (i) the motivation of low-rank OT as a scalable alternative to full-rank OT 
and (ii) the extension of transport clustering to non-square cost matrices (i.e. $n \neq m$).

A pitfall in the manuscript noted by all reviewers was the motivation for low-rank OT in the Introduction as a scalable alternative to full-rank OT. We agree with the reviewers that this motivation is confusing and misleading in regards to our work and have updated the manuscript to avoid this confusion (changes marked in red). While previous work [1, 2, 3] motivates low-rank OT as a practical approach for speeding up OT, these algorithms do not necessarily guarantee solution quality for low-rank OT, and scalability is an inappropriate point of comparison unless solution quality is guaranteed. Specifically, reviewer `njmU` noted the theoretical contradiction in motivating low-rank OT, an NP-hard optimization problem [2], as a scalable alternative to full-rank OT, a problem solved in polynomial-time. We agree with `njmU` entirely. The key value of transport clustering is not its scalability, but in showing the near equivalence of low-rank OT and $K$-means up to a full-rank OT registration. This near equivalence obviates the need for bespoke analysis of low-rank OT and instead inherits the well-studied guarantees of $K$-means.

Two of the reviewers also noted the lack of theoretical guarantees or empirical validation for the extension of transport clustering to the setting with arbitrary marginal distributions and $n \neq m$. In the rebuttal, we investigate this case  by applying transport clustering with Kantorovich registration to the 2-Moons and 8-Gaussians [4] dataset. On this dataset, we find that transport clustering with Kantorovich registration performs as well as the Monge case with a performance improvement to both both FRLC and LOT which is highly consistent across a range of $n \neq m$ (Table 1). While our theory is specific to Monge registration, we hope to complement the empirical efficacy of Kantorovich registration with theoretical results in future work.

[2] Meyer Scetbon and Marco Cuturi. _Low-rank Optimal Transport: Approximation, Statistics and Debiasing_. In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 2022.

[3] Peter Halmos, Xinhao Liu, Julian Gold, and Benjamin Raphael. _Low-Rank Optimal Transport through Factor Relaxation with Latent Coupling_. NeurIPS 2024.

[4] Alexander Tong, Nikolay Malkin, Guillaume Huguet, Yanlei Zhang, Jarrid Rector-Brooks, Kilian Fatras, Guy Wolf, and Yoshua Bengio. _Improving and generalizing flow-based generative models with minibatch optimal transport_. In ICML Workshop on New Frontiers in Learning, Control, and Dynamical Systems, 2023.

[5] Piotr Indyk and Eric Price. _K-median clustering, model-based compressive sensing, and sparse recovery for earth mover distance._ In STOC, pp. 627–636, 2011.

summary.value: The reviews are overall towards positive side, but the paper is still around the borderline. Unfortunately, I find that at least one of the major concerns are not adequately addressed during the rebuttal. I thus suggest to reject the paper.

reviewer_concerns.value:
The major concern raised by almost all reviewers, is about the efficiency of the algorithm, and in turn, the motivation to consider a computationally harder problem than the original one. I find this issue outstanding even after the rebuttal. Indeed, the rebuttal admits the efficiency problem. Unfortunately, the authors did not really suggest a solution, but to argue that they tend to ignore the efficiency issue and focus on building relationships between their problem and k-means. While I can see the contribution of reducing to k-means, but eventually this approach is not practical, which seems to be an issue for ICLR where potential of application is important.

The other issues seem to be minor and are more or less addressed.

reviewer_scores.value: I think the reviewers will keep the scores unchanged, because I think the major concern is not adequately addressed.
